title: Desmond Tutu
hookLine: a South African archbishop who preached against apartheid, then listened to the truth told at the Truth and Reconciliation Commission

lines: A HALL, A WITNESS, A MICROPHONE.
THE CHAIR PUTS HIS HEAD DOWN.
cards: What does the person in charge do when the testimony is too much to bear? A hall in South Africa: rows of chairs, microphones, headphones for translation.
A witness describes what was done to him in a police cell long before, and what it did to his family. At the long table facing him sits a small man in a bishop's purple shirt.
Partway through, he puts his head down on the table and weeps, in front of everyone. Then he lifts his head, and the hearing goes on. He chaired those hearings, and he insisted on hearing everything.

teach.b: Desmond Tutu was an Anglican priest who became archbishop of Cape Town.

Under apartheid, the system that separated South Africans by race and kept power in white hands, he preached that it was a sin, not just a bad policy, because every person is made in the image of God.
He marched, he buried the dead after massacres, he called on the world to put pressure on the government, and he laughed a great deal.
When apartheid ended, the new president, Nelson Mandela, asked him to chair the Truth and Reconciliation Commission. The idea was unusual. Victims would tell their stories in public, and be heard.

teach.h: THE WHOLE TRUTH, OR NO AMNESTY.
teach.b: People who had committed political crimes could ask for amnesty, but only if they told the whole truth about what they had done. Truth first. Then, maybe, reconciliation.

Tutu drew on the Bible for both halves. Jesus says, in the King James Bible, "And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free." And Paul writes that God "hath given to us the ministry of reconciliation."
Tutu often spoke of ubuntu, a southern African idea he explained as: a person becomes a person through other people. In his telling, if you dehumanize someone, you lose some of your own humanity too.
Forgiveness, he was clear, didn't mean forgetting, or pretending it wasn't so bad; forgiving starts with naming what was done. Not everyone agreed with the commission.
Some families felt amnesty let the people who killed their loved ones walk away, and they said so. Tutu listened to that too. He called the work unfinished.

how: Anglicans remember Desmond Tutu, and his writing on ubuntu, forgiveness and reconciliation is read in churches, schools and peace work.

games.q: you chair the hearings. a family says amnesty is letting their son's killer walk free. what do you do?
o: tell them the process is fair and move on.
listen, and admit the work is unfinished.
games.why: Tutu listened to critics of the commission too, and called the work of reconciliation unfinished.

practice: Bring to mind someone you're out of step with, a friend, a sibling, a parent, a colleague, and instead of rehearsing the argument, look for one plain true sentence about your own part: I was short with you, or I didn't call.
Hold it, and if you pray, bring that sentence and that person before God; if not, just keep the sentence.

wordCard.voice: Desmond Tutu. The archbishop who called apartheid a sin, and then chaired a commission built on telling the truth before seeking reconciliation.

orig.note: Greek: reconciliation, Paul's word in 2 Corinthians 5:18, 'the ministry of reconciliation.'

carryVoice: Your line: truth, then reconciliation. Forgiving isn't the same as forgetting. That's day nine hundred seventy.
